page: Vultr voc-m-4c-32gb-800s-amd is an instance within the Optimized Cloud Compute family, featuring 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 2 physical AMD EPYC cores with multithreading enabled. Operating at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz, the x86_64 processor includes 32 MB of L3 cache and supports advanced instruction sets such as AVX-512, VNNI, BF16, and SHA_ni cryptography. The system is equipped with 32.0 GB of system memory, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. Local storage is provided by an integrated 800 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark evaluations demonstrate strong single-core performance, with stress-ng single-core CPU testing placing the instance in the top 10%. Multi-core CPU performance and PassMark CPU scores align with the middle 50% average. Memory subsystem performance is characterized by an average read bandwidth of 142.68 GB/sec for large blocks, while large block write bandwidth is strong at 115.6 GB/sec, placing it in the top 25%. Single-threaded compression tasks perform well, with gzip compression reaching 31.95 GB/sec. However, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and PassMark database operations show weaker results, landing in the bottom 25%. For lightweight machine learning tasks, the instance achieves an average text generation speed of 143.22 tokens/sec on a small 135M model, though performance drops significantly on larger models.

From a resource density perspective, this instance offers a cost-efficient profile for memory-intensive workloads that do not require massive parallel compute. The high memory allocation of 32 GB paired with 800 GB of fast NVMe storage makes it highly suitable for memory-cached databases, Redis deployments, and moderate data processing pipelines. The primary tradeoff is the limited multi-core scaling, as evidenced by the average multi-core benchmarks and weaker multi-threaded decompression scores. Consequently, it is best suited for memory-bound applications, Redis caching layers, and general-purpose backend services rather than heavy parallel computing or high-throughput web serving.
